newsitem.title: USA: DC panel rejects mayor's FY'98 budget second time.
newsitem.headline: DC panel rejects mayor's FY'98 budget second time.

text.p: The District of Columbia's financial control board on Wednesday rejected for the second time a fiscal 1998 budget proposed by Mayor Marion Barry and said it would take control of developing a budget for the financially struggling city.

"The mayor is still reluctant to make the very hard choices" needed to achieve a balanced budget for the city that does not short change D.C. schools and citizen safety, Andrew Brimmer, chairman of the five-member board, said at a panel meeting.
Under the 1995 law that created the city's financial control board, Barry has two opportunities annually to propose a fiscal 1998 budget that meets the panel's approval.
On February 1, Barry proposed a $3.3 billion balanced budget plan that would have saved $50 million in fiscal 1998 through restructuring of about $300 million in city debt.
But the control board on March 3 said the plan did not provide enough funds for public safety and schools and gave Barry 15 days to overhaul the plan.

On March 18, Barry proposed a second $3.3 billion budget for the city, but the control board said on Wednesday that the new plan includes funding for the mayor's "own priorities rather than addressing more essential public service priorities."
Brimmer said the authority will take over the process and submit a revised budget shortly to the District's council for review.

"At this juncture, the authority has little choice except - yet again - to reject the Mayor's budget proposal," Brimmer said. "We are disappointed that the mayor has failed to present a realistic budget."

In other action, the panel voted to ask the U.S. Congress for an additional $54.9 million in the current fiscal year for needed D.C. school construction and repairs and to raise police salaries and other safety projects.
The panel also voted to take over disposing of 23 surplus public school properties, some of which have been vacant since the 1970s. The panel said Barry failed to adequately deal with the sites.
The panel also voted to continue to allow D.C.'s mayor to nominate an inspector general, but reduced the amount of time the mayor has to make the selection to 60 days.
